questions: Do most people who try drugs get addicted?
short: Mostly not, except tobacco. In a big US survey, about 9 in 100 people who'd tried cannabis were expected to become dependent at some point. Cocaine 21, alcohol 23, tobacco 68.
but: It's people's own memories, in one US survey from 2001 to 2005. People in prison, or who had died, weren't asked, so the real figures may be higher.

questions: Did the soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stay addicted?
short: Mostly not. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home, and 12 in 100 within 3 years.
but: Vietnam was unusual: heroin was cheap, pure and everywhere. The lead researcher says few of these young men would have become addicted at home.

questions: Why is it hard to pee on MDMA?
short: Nobody knows: no study has measured it. A water-holding hormone rose in 8 men on MDMA. Three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker.
but: None of these studies reported anything about pee. So nobody knows if the hormone has anything to do with it.

questions: Can a pill's logo or look tell you what's in it?
short: No study we read shows it can. In a Dutch check, about 40 in 100 online pill reports claimed over 10 mg more MDMA than lab tests found in matching pills.
but: No study we read measured how much pills with the same logo differ. And the online check is one Dutch study of two websites.

questions: What are NBOMes, and are they sold as LSD?
short: Yes, sometimes. NBOMes are lab-made drugs, mostly sold on blotters. In case reports up to 2014, several people who got sick or died thought they'd taken LSD.
but: These reports don't show how often 'LSD' blotters hold NBOMes. And they're reports of people who got sick, so they can't say how risky one use is.

questions: Are designer benzos like etizolam more dangerous?
short: Nobody has compared them with prescribed benzos. Of 141 deaths with a designer benzo in published reports, 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.
but: These reports only count people who got into trouble, not everyone who used. So they can't say how risky one use is.

questions: What does snorting coke do to your nose, and does it heal?
short: It can make a hole in the wall between your nostrils, and damage can spread. 126 of 127 people with this damage had that hole. Healing after stopping hasn't been studied.
but: These are people who already had damage and went to doctors. Nobody knows how many people who snort get it.

questions: Do benzos get you high, and who actually likes them?
short: It may depend on who you are. In one lab study, most of 36 people without drug problems chose a dummy pill over Valium. People with past drug problems almost always chose benzos.
but: People with past drug problems were tested in separate studies by another lab, mostly with much bigger doses. So we can't tell if their past made the difference.

questions: Why do people misuse Xanax and other benzos?
short: Mostly to relax or sleep, they say. In a big US survey, 47 in 100 people who misused benzos named relaxing as the main reason, 27 sleep, and 12 getting high.
but: It's what people told a survey. And 'misuse' here also counts taking more of your own pills than your doctor said.

questions: Is it dangerous to mix benzos like Xanax with alcohol?
short: Death records suggest so. In Finland, people who died with alcohol and the benzo temazepam had less alcohol in their blood. It was about a quarter less than in deaths from alcohol alone.
but: Only deaths were counted, and the two groups were different kinds of people. So this can't show how risky mixing is.

questions: Does Suboxone block other opioids, and for how long?
Does Suboxone block other opioids?
short: Only partly. In small lab studies, even high doses didn't fully block heroin or another opioid, and the block faded in the days after the last dose.
but: Each study had 3 to 10 volunteers dependent on heroin, not in treatment. Fentanyl and overdose weren't studied.

questions: Can Suboxone put you in withdrawal if you use fentanyl?
short: Many say so. In a US survey, 37 in 100 who took Suboxone's main drug after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal. After methadone, 15 in 100 did.
but: These are memories, not records. And the survey couldn't tell if Suboxone caused the withdrawal or just didn't ease it.

questions: What happens after stopping Suboxone?
short: About 5 in 100 people had an overdose treated by a doctor within 6 months of stopping, in US insurance records. Nearly half went to an emergency department.
but: People who died were left out, so fatal overdoses aren't counted. And nobody stayed on Suboxone to compare with.

questions: Can tramadol cause seizures, and what happens in an overdose?
short: In overdoses, seizures are common. 11 in 100 people treated at one Australian unit had them, and about 35 in 100 in Iran. Some had trouble breathing too.
but: These were overdoses, often with other pills too. For normal doses, the studies we read have only reports of seizures, not how often they happen.

questions: Is tramadol withdrawal different from other opioids?
short: Sometimes, going by reports. In US reports from 1995 to 2000, most looked like usual opioid withdrawal. But about 1 in 8 also had panic, confusion, numbness or hallucinations.
but: It's only cases people chose to report. And there was no group stopping other opioids to compare with.

questions: Adderall or Ritalin: which works better, and which has more side effects?
short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Quitting over side effects didn't clearly differ between them.
but: Few trials tested the two head to head, and none in adults. Most compared one drug with a dummy pill, for a few weeks.

questions: Is psychosis more likely on Adderall than Ritalin?
short: A bit, in one big US study. But it's rare either way. Each year, about 3 in 1,000 people on amphetamine (as in Adderall) had it, against 2 on methylphenidate (as in Ritalin).
but: It's one study of insurance records, not a trial. Things the records missed, like drug use or early signs of illness, could explain part of it.

questions: How long do drugs show up on a drug test?
short: It varies a lot. An expert review says most drugs show in urine for 1.5 to 4 days after one use. In one study, some regular weed smokers were still positive on day 30.
but: The usual figures come from tiny studies. Some had just one or two people, given one dose in a lab.

questions: Can medicines cause a false positive on a drug test?
short: Yes, some can, on certain tests. On one benzo test, 46 of 50 people taking the HIV drug efavirenz screened positive, but a lab check found no benzos.
but: Most reports describe one or a few people, or a medicine added to urine in a lab. For most medicines, we don't know how often it happens.

questions: Can a drug test miss fentanyl, or benzos like Xanax?
short: Yes. A 2017 expert review says standard opiate tests don't react to fentanyl. Most benzo tests can miss Xanax (alprazolam) unless the lab adds an extra step.
but: This is about urine tests, from expert reviews dated 2004 to 2017, not new studies. They give no numbers on how often a drug is missed, and tests change.
